title: What Actually Causes Déjà Vu?
voiceover: Why does a new place feel strangely familiar? Déjà vu is common: about 60 percent of people have experienced it. In 2003, Alan Brown reviewed the research in Psychological Bulletin. He found explanations fall into four groups: dual processing, neurological, memory and attentional. That means researchers still have several competing explanations. One memory-based idea is that a scene resembles one you've seen before, but you can't recall it. In 2012, Anne Cleary's team tested it in virtual reality. Scenes with the same layout as an earlier scene felt more familiar when people couldn't recall that earlier scene. They also reported more déjà vu. So déjà vu may be a familiarity signal firing without a memory to go with it. Tomorrow: do search engines change how you remember?

description: Why does a new place feel strangely familiar? About 60% of people have had déjà vu, researchers have several competing explanations, and a virtual-reality study supports a scene-layout idea. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Brown, A. S. (2003). A review of the déjà vu experience. Psychological Bulletin, 129(3), 394-413. Source: Cleary, A. M., Brown, A. S., Sawyer, B. D., Nomi, J. S., Ajoku, A. C., & Ryals, A. J. (2012). Familiarity from the configuration of objects in 3-dimensional space and its relation to déjà vu: A virtual reality investigation. Consciousness and Cognition, 21(2), 969-975.
accuracy_note: UNSETTLED. Brown (2003) organizes explanations into four categories; none is established as the single cause. Cleary et al. (2012) is one lab study in virtual reality supporting one idea (Gestalt familiarity). The video states this as 'may'.
